title: When a Preference Becomes a Rule

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Imagine your team gathers partner feedback in one short meeting. The quickest speakers shape the discussion, and written comments arrive after the decision. Everyone was invited. Does that mean everyone had a useful chance to contribute?

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: Not necessarily. People had to attend at that time, read quickly, and speak before we moved on. Those may be familiar habits, but they're worth questioning.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: That's the focus here: noticing when a preference becomes a rule. Let's follow the work from an invitation to a decision, and see what we could make easier.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: This matters in service conversations too. Suppose someone uses a communication device and brings a friend. It might feel faster to ask the friend everything, but we'd miss the person's own voice.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: We can ask the person how they'd like their friend involved and allow time for their response. A supporter's presence doesn't tell us who makes decisions. We need to check the actual responsibilities.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: And relationships and independence don't have to compete. The person can value support and still be central to the conversation.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Back at the partner meeting, what would you change first?

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: I'd rewrite the invitation in plain language. What are we deciding? What can input change? When do we need it? I'd explain the abbreviations and give people a clear contact for questions or communication support.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: That gives people a starting point. Patience helps, and so do an accessible document and appropriate language support. One doesn't replace the other.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: Should we just offer every possible way to respond?

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: I'd ask what would actually help. More options can be useful, but three extra forms could create more work. Perhaps a clear draft, written comments, and a discussion would meet the need. We also need someone to read and respond to what we invite.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: So inclusion includes the follow-through. A comment box isn't much help if nobody can tell what happened to the comments.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: The Equity Analysis Toolkit can help us think this through. What's the purpose? Who's affected? What do we know about the difficulty, and whose experience haven't we heard? Then compare a few practical options.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: If a few people ask for an online form, that's useful feedback. It doesn't prove a single online route works for everyone. We can ask about other needs and be honest about what we still don't know.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: Let's propose a small trial. Send the draft early, offer two useful ways to comment, name who responds, and set a date to review how it went. Take it to the person who can approve the change.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: I'd also talk with colleagues about the workload. If nobody has time to respond, we haven't finished planning. The arrangement needs to work for the staff doing it and the people using it.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: How would you judge the trial? Attendance alone won't tell us whether people influenced the decision.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: I'd check whether comments arrived in time, whether concerns received an explanation, and whether the new options created extra burden. Ask participants what helped. Use the information we need without collecting unnecessary personal details.

turns.speaker: host1
turns.text: For a practice step, choose one routine in your work. What's its purpose? Who finds it difficult? What assumption should you check? Write one change, who needs to approve it, and how you'll tell whether it helped. Pause and take your time.

turns.speaker: geffen
turns.text: That's how the four courses fit together: notice your reaction, question a familiar expectation, listen to the person, and follow through. Start with one improvement you can explain. Let what people tell you help shape the next step.
